summary: A proposal from BBN to add a way to resynchronize the status of a single connection in the ARPANET Host-Host protocol. Without it, a lost or corrupted control message could leave the two ends confused, for example the lost allocate and half-closed problems, and the only fix was to reset every connection between two hosts. It was answered in RFC 492.

plainLanguage.summary: If two people on a phone line disagree about whether the call is still on, there was no way to fix that one call. This proposed a fix without hanging up on all calls.

questions: what is the lost allocate problem
what are rcs and rcr commands
subtitle: A proposal to repair a single ARPANET connection whose two ends disagree, without resetting everything.

tldr.problem: If a host is interrupted or a control message is lost, the two ends of a connection disagree about its state, and the Host-Host protocol had no way to repair it.
tldr.mechanism: Two new commands, RCS (reset connection by sender) and RCR (reset connection by receiver), zero the allocation variables at both ends. The meanings of RTS, STR and ERR are also changed so half-closed connections get closed.
tldr.outcome: The authors argue the data stream is preserved, so resynchronizing is safe at any time, and that the protocol would become far more robust.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 467 as Unknown, and it is updated by RFC 492. It is a 1973 proposal for the Host-Host protocol.

sections.title: The Problem: Inconsistent Connection State
sections.content:
The Host-Host protocol had no provision for resynchronizing the status information kept at the two ends of a connection. After a service interruption, or a control message lost or corrupted in an interface or the subnet, the two NCPs stay confused forever.

One symptom is the lost allocate: the receiver believes bit and message allocations are outstanding, while the sender believes it has none, so data can never flow again. The RST command is inappropriate because it destroys all connections between the two hosts. The other symptom is the half-closed connection, where one NCP thinks the connection is open and the other thinks it is closed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people disagree whether the call is still on, and the only fix was hanging up every call between them.

sections.title: The RCS and RCR Commands
sections.content:
Two new commands, each an 8-bit command code followed by an 8-bit link, are proposed. RCS (reset connection by sender) goes from the host sending on the link to the host receiving on it. RCR (reset connection by receiver) goes the other way. The sender might use RCS after a timeout with traffic to move but no allocation, or when an inconsistent event occurs, such as an outstanding allocation above 2^32 bits or 2^16 messages.

Resynchronizing means emptying messages and allocates from the pipeline, zeroing the bit and message allocation variables at both ends, and restarting the normal allocate and message exchange. Because RCS and RCR work as a positive acknowledgement pair, the scheme is race-free.
sections.plainLanguage: Two special 'reset' notes, one for each side, let either person say 'let us start counting again from zero'.

sections.title: Sender, Receiver and Simultaneous Resynchronization
sections.content:
A sender starts by entering a waiting-for-RCR-reply state, waiting until a RFNM has been received for every regular message sent, then sending RCS. The receiver zeros its allocation variables, returns to readiness to accept a message, replies RCR, and may send an ALL command for any allocation it wants. On the RCR reply, the sender zeros its variables and becomes ready to send.

A receiver can start the same sequence by sending RCR, for example when a TIP or TELNET user expects output but gets none. The sender waits for its pipeline to empty, zeros its variables and answers with RCS.

If both ends start at once, the RCS and RCR cross in the pipeline and each end treats the other's command as the reply, so the result is correct regardless of timing.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever notices the problem says 'reset', the other waits until everything in flight is done, agrees, and both start fresh. If both say it at once, they just agree.

sections.title: Half-Closed Connections
sections.content:
A long interruption can leave one end open and the other closed, perhaps because the user unilaterally dissolved the connection by sending CLS and closing without waiting for the acknowledgement, which is legal only if the subnet indicates the destination is dead. The proposal changes the meaning of three existing commands rather than adding new ones.

If the open end keeps sending, the closed end replies with an ERR saying the link is unknown (error code 5), and the open end then closes the connection in its tables without sending CLS. If the closed end sends an RTS or STR naming the same foreign socket as an existing open connection, the open end closes the old connection first, again without CLS, and then responds.
sections.plainLanguage: If one friend hung up but the other did not notice, the first one's reply makes the second one hang up too, so both agree again.

messages.label: RCS
messages.note: Sent once a RFNM has arrived for every regular message.

messages.label: RCR
messages.note: Confirms the reset after zeroing its allocation variables.
